 1             I. INTRODUCTION, QUALIFICATIONS, AND RESPONSIBILITIES

 2   Q1.     Would you please state your name and address?
 3   A.      My name is Jamal Mamkhezri. My business address is Mamkhezri Consulting LLC, 2010
 4   North Park Drive, Las Cruces, New Mexico, 88005.

 5   Q2.     Where are you employed?
 6   A.      I am employed by New Mexico State University (“NMSU”) in the Department of
 7   Economics, Applied Statistics, and International Business in the College of Business. I am a Full
 8   Professor and hold the Chevron Endowed Professorship in Economics. I also serve as Graduate
 9   Director of the MA in Economics program and Associate Director of the Center for Public Utilities
10   (“CPU”) at NMSU. NMSU is the only university in the country that houses both a National
11   Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (“NARUC”)-endorsed training institute and
12   graduate degree programs with a concentration in public utility regulation, including the nationally
13   recognized Public Utility Regulation and Economics (“PURE”) certificate. I also hold an
14   affiliation as Visiting Research Faculty with the Energy Policy and Innovation Center
15   (“EPIcenter”) at the Georgia Institute of Technology. For the purposes of this proceeding, I am
16   engaged by the New Mexico Department of Justice (“NMDOJ”), through Mamkhezri Consulting
17   LLC, to provide expert testimony on El Paso Electric Company’s (“EPE”) proposed non-standard
18   rate offerings, its proposed Large Load Tariff, its proposed migration of battery capacity costs
19   from the Renewable Portfolio Standard (“RPS”) Cost Rider to base rates, and the arithmetic
20   verification of specific quantitative claims in EPE’s filing. The expert opinions expressed in this
21   testimony are my own and do not necessarily reflect the views of NMSU, the CPU, or Georgia
22   Tech.

23   Q3.     Would you please describe your educational and professional qualifications?
24   A.      I received a Ph.D. in Economics in 2019. My research and professional work concentrate
25   on energy and environmental economics, applied econometrics, electricity-rate analysis, and
26   public preferences for energy and utility policies. I have published more than thirty peer-reviewed
27   articles in journals including Energy Economics, The Energy Journal, Energy Policy, Utilities
28   Policy, Applied Energy, and Energy Research and Social Science, among others. I currently serve

30   for Energy Economics (“USAEE”). Through my role at the CPU, I have participated in nationally
31   recognized rate-case training programs offered by NMSU and attended by regulatory professionals
32   from across the United States, programs which are endorsed by NARUC.

33   Q4.    Have you previously filed testimony before the New Mexico Public Regulation
34   Commission (“NMPRC” or “Commission”)?
35   A.     Yes. On August 14, 2026, I filed direct testimony on behalf of the NMDOJ in Southwestern
36   Public Service Company’s annual 2027 renewable energy portfolio procurement plan proceeding,
37   Docket No. 26-0000132.

38   Q5.    Is the NMDOJ sponsoring any other witnesses in this case whose testimony you rely
39   on?
40   A.     Yes. Dr. Doug Gegax is filing Direct Testimony on behalf of the NMDOJ in this case
41   addressing EPE’s proposed class base-revenue allocations, banding and gradualism, and standard-
42   service rate design for the residential and small general service classes, including the residential
43   Customer Charge. My testimony is designed to complement his; I offer no independent
44   recommendation on class revenue allocation or standard-service rate design, and where those
45   subjects intersect my analysis, I rely on and cross-reference his testimony. One qualification:
46   where a change in recovery mechanism that is within my scope carries a class-allocation
47   consequence, I quantify that consequence from EPE’s own filed allocation factors, as I do in
48   Question 41; and where the choice of mechanism is itself the choice of allocation basis, as it is for
49   the battery capacity costs in Questions 41 through 43, I say which mechanism I recommend and
50   why. I offer no view on the allocation factors EPE derives in its class cost-of-service study or on
51   their application to any other cost, which are Dr. Gegax’s subjects. The NMDOJ does not sponsor
52   an overall revenue-requirement witness in this case; where EPE’s requested revenue increase
53   enters my analysis, I use EPE’s filed figures without endorsing them. I take them as given only for
54   the purposes of my analysis; I have not tested them and take no position on whether they are
55   correct.

56   Q6.     What is the purpose of your testimony?
57   A.      My testimony addresses four subjects that arise from EPE’s Application and affect
58   residential and small commercial customers: EPE’s three proposed new non-standard rate
59   offerings (the Low-Income Rider, the Peak Time Rebate Pilot under Rate No. 52, and the Time-
60   of-Day (“TOD”) modifications, including the new Experimental Off-Peak Demand Rate); EPE’s
61   proposed Large Load Tariff (Rate Nos. 50 and 51), measured against the safeguards other state
62   commissions have adopted for comparable service; EPE’s proposal to migrate battery capacity
63   costs from the RPS Cost Rider into base rates; and arithmetic verification of specific quantitative
64   claims in EPE’s filing. Class base-revenue allocation, banding, and standard-service rate design
65   for the residential and small general service classes are addressed in the Direct Testimony of Dr.
66   Gegax. Nothing in my testimony endorses EPE’s requested revenue requirement; where my
67   analysis uses it, I assume it only for that purpose and take no position on it.

68   Q7.     Are you sponsoring any exhibits with your testimony?
69   A.      Yes. I am sponsoring Exhibit JM-1, the calculations workbook that supports my testimony.
70   It contains the workpapers underlying the dollar and percentage figures and the tables in my
71   testimony, organized by sheet: the class cost-of-service figures drawn from EPE’s filed schedules
72   (Sheet 01), the arithmetic items in EPE’s filing (Sheet 02), the Large Load Tariff cost-shift analysis
73   (Sheet 03, with parallel public-data and BorderPlex-actual versions on Sheets 04 and 05), the Large
74   Load design-feature comparison across jurisdictions (Sheet 06), and the battery cost-recovery
75   analysis (Sheet 07).

76   Q8.     Please summarize your recommendations.
77   A.      I recommend the Commission:
78   (i)    approve the Low-Income Rider, whose intra-class recovery arithmetic I have verified, on the
79          condition that EPE finalize its State data-sharing arrangement, estimate and track its
80          administrative cost, and report enrollment and cost experience in its next general rate case;
81   (ii)   approve the Peak Time Rebate Pilot with the refinements described in Question 17;
82   (iii) order opt-out TOD rates rather than EPE’s proposed opt-in design, consistent with the opt-
83          out proposal EPE filed in compliance with the Commission’s Order Denying Petition for
84          Variance in Case No. 20-00104-UT (August 31, 2022), while preserving a straightforward

 85          opt-back-out path, explained on the customer’s bill, for customers who cannot shift load out
 86          of the on-peak window, including elderly customers and those relying on medical equipment,
 87          with any revenue shortfall deferred for review and true-up against actual experience, and
 88          evaluate the proposed seasonal differential as cost-based seasonal rate design rather than as
 89          a demand-response measure;
 90   (iv) approve the Experimental Off-Peak Demand Rate as filed;
 91   (v)    condition approval of Large Load Tariff Rate Nos. 50 and 51 on the eight strengthening
 92          conditions described in Questions 31 through 37, being an 85 percent minimum billing
 93          demand, which binds above roughly 35,300 kW of contract capacity under Rate No. 50,
 94          paired with a minimum-charge provision, minimum collateral of $520,000 per MW at the
 95          outset of service with no discretionary acceptance of unrated credit support, termination
 96          damages reformulated as the net present value of the remaining demand-charge revenue and
 97          floored at net book value, a but-for Contribution-in-Aid-of-Construction (“CIAC”) standard
 98          above $5 million, behind-the-meter (“BTM”) provisions, an explicit cost-allocation finding
 99          reaching the full incremental cost of service, annual classification testing on metered demand
100          and load factor during the Load Ramp Period with reclassification to Rate No. 51 if the load
101          factor falls short, and pre-execution filing of each Energy Service Agreement with the
102          Commission with an opportunity for Staff and intervenors to object; and
103   (vi)   retain the Santa Teresa and Carne battery capacity costs in the RPS Cost Rider, which avoids
104          shifting approximately $1.82 million per year onto the Residential class, while accepting that
105          the Buena Vista 1 costs move to base rates as directed in the Recommended Decision in Case
106          No. 19-00348-UT, without accepting EPE’s proposed jurisdictional allocation of the Buena
107          Vista 1 costs, and conditioning any battery capacity costs placed in base rates on a continued
108          reconciliation mechanism and a demonstration of the residential class-allocation effect.

110   record, none of which changes a proposed rate. On class base-revenue allocation, banding, and

113                                 II. SUMMARY OF EPE’S APPLICATION

114   Q9.      Would you please summarize EPE’s proposed increase in New Mexico retail base
115   revenues in this case?
116   A.       EPE seeks to increase its non-fuel base rate revenues in New Mexico by $70.4 million on
117   a net basis, comprising a $70.6 million non-fuel base rate revenue deficiency offset by a $0.2
118   million reduction in miscellaneous service revenue, as those amounts appear in Schedule O-1
119   (Total Revenue Requirement by Rate Classification) of the Amended Filing. 1 That deficiency
120   corresponds to a system-average increase of 50.4 percent on the Schedule O-1 determinants. EPE
121   instead states $70.7 million and 50.5 percent, computed from Schedules A-1 (Jurisdictional Cost
122   of Service) and A-2 (Summary of Revenue Change by Rate Class). The filing contradicts itself:
123   Schedule A-1’s increase exceeds Schedule O-1’s by $116,977, and EPE prints the system-average
124   percentage two different ways, 50.483 percent in Mr. Carrasco’s testimony and 50.531 percent at
125   Schedule A-2, line 4, neither of which matches the 50.399 percent the Schedule O-1 determinants
126   produce. 2 I set these items out in Table JM-01 and their arithmetic in Exhibit JM-1. None of them
127   changes a proposed rate. I raise them so that the record is internally consistent, not because the
128   dollars are material at the scale of this case; the smaller inconsistencies I found are recorded in
129   Exhibit JM-1 rather than developed here.
130            EPE’s current base rates were approved in Case No. 20-00104-UT on a calendar-year 2019
131   historic test year. 3 EPE’s 2026 Rate Case relies on a twelve-month Base Period ending September
132   30, 2025, adjusted under Rule 530.

133   Q10. Is EPE proposing to implement the full increase in a single step?
134   A.       No. EPE proposes a two-phase implementation. Phase 1 is proposed to take effect on
135   January 1, 2027 and represents a system-average increase of approximately 26.8 percent, with six
136   rate classes phased. That figure is a system average across all classes, so an individual class’s

153   Q11. How does your testimony relate to the Direct Testimony of Dr. Gegax?
154   A.      Dr. Gegax presents the NMDOJ’s analysis of EPE’s proposed class base-revenue
155   allocations and the banding and gradualism framework, together with the NMDOJ’s
156   recommendations on standard-service rate design for the residential and small general service
157   classes, including the residential Customer Charge. Two of his conclusions frame my analysis:
158   EPE’s proposed overall base-revenue increase of approximately 50 percent and approximately 73
159   percent residential at-full-cost increase are among the largest in recent New Mexico rate cases, and
160   the Commission’s long-standing practice of rate mitigation through banding should not be
161   abandoned in this case. The protections I recommend for the Large Load Tariff and the corrections
162   I recommend to the non-standard rate offerings operate within whatever class revenue levels and
163   standard-service rate designs the Commission adopts from Dr. Gegax’s testimony.

164   Q12. EPE states at Carrasco Direct Question 64 (Amended Filing at 50 (PDF page 53))
165   that “the proposed Customer Charge represents approximately 15% of the base rate
166   charges, which means that residential customers will continue to control 85% of the base
167   rate charges on their monthly bill.” Is that statement arithmetically correct?
168   A.     No. The proposed Phase 2 Customer Charge of $19.17 per month, applied to EPE’s test-
169   year 1,180,224 residential customer-months, generates annual Customer Charge revenue of
170   $22,624,894, against a Phase 2 at-full-cost residential class revenue requirement of $126,774,619
171   on Schedule A-2 and $126,735,163 on Schedule O-1. The ratio is 17.85 percent on either, not 15
172   percent, so residential customers would control 82.15 percent of their monthly base-rate bill
173   through usage rather than 85 percent. That ratio counts the Customer Charge as it is billed to every
174   residential customer, which is the first of three conventions for measuring it. The second
175   convention sets aside the $1.04 that EPE adds to the charge to pay for the Low-Income Rider I
176   describe in Question 14 and uses only the $18.139 cost-based component EPE identifies, which
177   gives 16.89 percent. The third convention measures what EPE would collect. The Rider is a
178   provision of Rate No. 01 that EPE describes and models as a credit equal to the Customer Charge:
179   a qualifying customer is billed the $19.17 Customer Charge and credited the same $19.17, so that
180   customer pays no Customer Charge. EPE assumes 5,329 qualifying customers, which is 63,948
181   customer-months a year. Of the $22,624,894 billed, EPE therefore collects $21,399,011, and on
182   that amount the ratio is 16.88 percent. I use the first convention, 17.85 percent, because it is the
183   charge EPE filed and the charge that appears on the bill. On all three the ratio lies between 16.88
184   and 17.85 percent, and on all three it exceeds EPE’s 15 percent. The 2.85 percentage-point
185   overstatement is not large in absolute terms, but it is large enough that the Commission should not
186   credit EPE’s 15 percent and 85 percent figures as filed. At the 720 kWh a month Mr. Carrasco
187   identifies as the residential class average, the proposed Customer Charge is 17.9 percent of the
188   base-rate bill on EPE’s own annual-average residential table, which is the class ratio; the share is
189   higher for customers using less and lower for those using more, running from 41.4 percent at 250
190   kWh to 14.3 percent at 1,000 kWh (Exhibit MC-02 to the Direct Testimony of Manuel Carrasco
191   Amended Filing, tab C, Bills Default Ph 2, annual-average residential table). EPE’s approximately
192   15 percent corresponds to a customer using roughly 950 kWh a month, about 30 percent above the

200   Q13. Would you please summarize the three new non-standard rate offerings EPE
201   proposes in this case?
202   A.         EPE proposes three new non-standard rate offerings in addition to the standard-service
203   rate-design changes and the Large Load Tariff. The three are (a) a new Low-Income Rider under

205   households; (b) a new two-year Peak Time Rebate Pilot Program filed as Rate No. 52, offering
206   Residential customers a bill credit for reducing usage during EPE-called peak events; and (c)
207   modifications to EPE’s TOD rates, including a new Experimental Off-Peak Demand Rate for two
208   commercial classes and a question regarding opt-in versus opt-out structure. 5

209   A. Low-Income Rider

210   Q14. Would you please describe the proposed Low-Income Rider?
211   A.       EPE proposes to add a Low-Income Rider provision to Rate No. 01 that waives the entire
212   monthly Customer Charge for qualifying customers, meaning residential customers authorized to
213   receive benefits under either the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (“SNAP”) or the Low
214   Income Home Energy Assistance Program (“LIHEAP”) in New Mexico. The credit equals the
215   prevailing Residential Customer Charge dollar-for-dollar, $14.56 in Phase 1 and $19.17 in Phase
216   2 under EPE’s proposal. EPE would identify those customers through the New Mexico Health
217   Care Authority client database. 6 EPE proposes to recover the cost intra-class by embedding a $1.04
218   per month incremental component in the Customer Charge paid by non-qualifying residential
219   customers. 7 EPE estimates approximately 5,329 LIHEAP-eligible customers and total annual
220   discount of approximately $931,000 in Phase 1 and $1.2 million in Phase 2.

221   Q15. What is your overall view of the Low-Income Rider?
222   A.       The Low-Income Rider is a useful affordability mechanism, and I recommend the
223   Commission approve it, subject to the program-integrity conditions I describe below. I verified
224   EPE’s arithmetic against its rate design model and its proof of revenue, and it holds: EPE derives
225   the Residential Customer Charge by dividing the customer-related revenue requirement allocated
226   to the class by the non-qualifying customer determinants, which for Phase 2 is $21,402,216 divided
227   by 1,116,276 customer-months, the 1,180,224 test-year customer-months less the 63,948 months
228   of the 5,329 assumed participants, and produces the $19.17 EPE filed. On that rounded charge the
229   1,116,276 non-qualifying customer-months recover $21,399,011 against the $21,402,216
230   requirement, so the non-qualifying customers who pay the charge fund the discount in full, to
231   within a $3,205 residual that is simply a rounding of the charge rather than a methodological
232   shortfall. 8

233            The 2025 amendment to the Public Utility Act, whose operative language Mr. Rene
234   Gonzalez quotes, authorizes the Commission to approve rates and programs designed to reduce
235   the burden of energy costs on low-income customers. That amendment is what makes a rider of
236   this kind available: before it, the statute’s low-income authority reached only energy efficiency
237   programs under the Efficient Use of Energy Act, not rates. 9 The design has the operational
238   advantage of using the State’s SNAP/LIHEAP eligibility determination rather than requiring EPE
239   to verify income independently, and the intra-class recovery mechanism keeps the cost from
240   spreading to non-residential classes, which is consistent with the principle of cost causation.
241            The Commission should attach program-integrity conditions, because EPE has
242   acknowledged in discovery that it has not yet finalized the SNAP and LIHEAP data-sharing
243   arrangement on which the rider depends, has not estimated the cost of administering it, and would
244   consider terminating the rider if participation runs materially above its estimate. 10 The
245   Commission should therefore direct EPE to finalize the State data-sharing arrangement, to estimate
246   and track the administrative cost, and to report enrollment and cost experience in its next general
247   rate case, so the rider’s costs stay visible to both participating and non-participating residential
248   customers. EPE’s discovery response arrives at the $1.04 add-on by arithmetic that spreads the
249   annual discount across the customer determinants of the entire Residential class, while its
250   workpaper derives the charge on the non-qualifying determinants. The two are the same
251   calculation expressed two ways and produce the same $1.04, so I recommend no correction; I note
252   the equivalence so the record is clear. My verification is of the derivation, not the level: it takes as
253   given the customer-related revenue requirement EPE allocates to the class, which is outside my
254   scope, and the level of the residential Customer Charge itself is addressed by Dr. Gegax. On EPE’s
255   filed inputs, the charge implements the rider correctly, and I recommend no adjustment to the
256   mechanism.

257   B. Peak Time Rebate Pilot Program (Rate No. 52)

258   Q16. Would you please describe the Peak Time Rebate Pilot?
259   A.         EPE proposes a two-year, summer-only voluntary pilot under which Residential Service

261   a baseline during EPE-called four-hour peak events from 3:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. on summer
262   weekdays. 11 The credit equals the kWh reduction multiplied by EPE’s avoided cost of energy
263   under the On-Peak Monthly Energy Payment Rate filed in Rate No. 16 Purchased Power Service.
264   EPE proposes a maximum of twenty events per summer, with each event a four-hour window from
265   3:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m., and no consecutive-day events beyond two. Customers who do not reduce
266   or who increase usage during an event receive no credit but are not penalized.

267   Q17. What is your view of the Peak Time Rebate Pilot?
268   A.         The pilot’s design is reasonable and its scope is modest. My concern is the credit rate. Rate
269   No. 52 sets the credit at the On-Peak Monthly Energy Payment Rate in Rate No. 16, which is the
270   rate EPE pays a qualifying facility for energy. The proposed tariff states no dollar value for that
271   rate, as I explain below, so a customer cannot tell from the tariff what a reduced kWh would earn.
272   The rate prices energy only. It carries no capacity value, even though reductions delivered during
273   called events, on summer afternoons between 3:00 p.m. and 7:00 p.m., are what relieves EPE’s
274   system peak, so ratepayers taking advantage of this pilot should also be credited with reducing
275   EPE’s capacity requirements. EPE’s own proposed TOD rates price an on-peak kWh in that same
276   window at 2.90 times the off-peak rate (Question 18 sets out the rates). Those two prices measure
277   different things, embedded cost recovery on the one hand and avoided energy cost on the other,
278   but their distance shows how little the pilot offers for the behavior it is meant to induce. The
279   remedy is not to credit at the retail on-peak rate: a customer who curtails already saves the retail
280   energy charge on every kWh not consumed, so a retail-level credit on top of that saving would
281   exceed any measure of avoided cost, and the excess would be recovered from customers who do
282   not participate. The remedy is a credit set between the two, above EPE’s avoided energy cost and
283   below the retail rate, which is what the second, higher credit tier in my recommendations is
284   designed to test.
